newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan people march against social disorder.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan people march against social disorder.

text.p: More than 50,000 demonstrators on Sunday lay on the boulevard in front of Taiwan's presidential office in a mass protest against the government's failure to check a spate of violent crimes.

Shocked by the recent kidnap and murder of a famous actress's teenage daughter, the protesters demanded the resignation of Premier Lien Chan while wielding cardboard signs that read "outrage" and "grieve".
"Apologise, (President) Lee Teng-Hui! Step down, Lien Chan!" the throng shouted in unison before lying down in front of a heavily manned police barricade.
"We do not want to see Taiwan become extinct. So we demand a reshuffle of the cabinet," a protest leader read a prepared statement using four languages spoken by various ethnic groups in Taiwan.

In the latest of a string of violent crimes that have hit Taiwan in the past year, police last month found the body of 17-year-old Pai Hsiao-yen, daughter of actress Pai Ping-ping, floating naked in a river.
The kidnappers, who remained at large, had strangled the teenager with two ropes, bound her hands and sunk her in the river with weights.
Activists said the murder was a stark example of how the government was failing to protect its people.
"We simply cannot be silent students anymore. We demand that the government start taking responsibility for the deterioration of social values," said a college student who joined the march.
Organisers had expected about 20,000 people to participate in the march. But unofficial estimates put the crowd at more than 50,000.
The rally, despite the presence of several party banners, remained largely non-political.

"This is a movement for all people. I urge all political organisations to abandon individual opinions and refrain from asserting all opinions not having to do with social reforms," said Lin Yi-hsiung, a protester and a prominent member of the opposition Democratic Progressive Party.
Interior Minister Lin Feng-cheng acknowledged in December that Taiwan's social order had deteriorated to a "shocking" level, with the crime rate soaring by 80 percent between 1990 to 1996.
In November 1996, two gunmen broke into the home of northern Taoyuan county magistrate Liu Pang-yu and killed eight people, including Liu, in a gangland-style attack.
One week later, women's rights activist Peng Wan-ju was raped and stabbed to death in southern Kaohsiung. Police found 35 knife wounds in her naked body.
President Lee on Friday apologised through his chief of staff for the "worsening social law and order", and said his government would take full responsbility.
But Huang Kun-huei, Lee's chief of staff, did not say what actions Lee planned to take.
Premier Lien, who is also vice president, has not spoken publically about Pai Hsiao-yen's murder.
